entries.text: The null/floor control uses 200 language-model-generated sequences without brain data to select words; the Methods describe matched predicted word times, a 10-candidate beam, and random rather than fMRI-likelihood ranking.
entries.condition: Compared with the actual stimulus words for the language-similarity floor; Methods note brain-predicted word times are retained.
entries.quote: A floor for each metric was computed by scoring the mean similarity between the actual stimulus words and 200 null sequences generated from a language model without using any brain data.

entries.text: Cross-subject decoding was barely above chance. Alignment used volumetric mapping through the MNI template to the target subject and surface-based source-to-target vertex mapping.
entries.value: Barely above chance; volumetric and surface-based anatomical alignment
entries.condition: Cross-subject models trained on other subjects and evaluated on target-subject responses; seven subjects contributed to the analysis.
entries.quote: Decoders trained on cross-subject data ( Extended Data Fig. 6 ) performed barely above chance, and significantly worse than decoders trained on within-subject data ( q ( FDR ) < 0.05 , two-sided t -test).

entries.text: Imagined-story identity was correctly identified with 100% accuracy across five reference stories.

entries.text: For four silent short films, decoded sequences were significantly more similar than chance to language descriptions for visually impaired viewers; the paper also reports qualitatively accurate event descriptions.

entries.quote: We compared the decoded word sequences to language descriptions of the films for the visually impaired (see Methods ), and found that they were significantly more similar than expected by chance ( q ( FDR ) < 0.05 , one-sided nonparametric test; Extended Data Fig. 5a ).

entries.condition: Direct classification; one class per vocabulary word

This way the
model outputs a one dimensional vector of probabilities of

entries.text: GPT-2 generates from an initial context, guided by GloVe embeddings of the decoder's top-five word predictions as anchor points that bias next-token scores; the decoded words are not simply supplied as the literal prompt.
entries.value: Top-five decoded words used as anchor points
entries.condition: GPT-2 next-token generation from an initial context; token scores adjusted by cosine similarity to decoder-derived anchors
entries.quote:
Our classiﬁcation decoder ﬁnds anchor points
for the language generation model (GPT-2), which generates
the next token given some initial context.

entries.text: No forward encoding model is described for scoring candidate text against brain responses; the described adjustment compares GPT-2 token words with decoded-word anchors in GloVe space.
entries.condition: GPT-2 language-generation method

entries.condition: Direct classification in the leave-one-subject-out setup; final results on 14 test subjects, with the target subject unseen during training

questions.q: What is the exact BERTScore for each subject on the perceived speech test story, and how does it compare to the null and translation ceiling?
questions.answer: Subject 1: 0.8077, Subject 2: 0.8104, Subject 3: 0.8116; Null: 0.7899; Translation ceiling: 0.8797. Decoder performs ~20% as well as translation system relative to null floor.

questions.q: What percentage of time-points were significantly decoded under BERTScore, and what was the identification accuracy percentile rank?
questions.answer: 72-82% of time-points significantly higher than chance (q(FDR)<0.05); mean percentile rank 0.85-0.91 for identification from other time-points.

questions.q: What evidence supports the claim that multiple cortical regions redundantly represent language at word/phrase granularity?
questions.answer: All 6 region-hemisphere combinations significantly decoded under WER/BERTScore (q(FDR)<0.05); pairwise decoded sequence similarities significantly above chance (q(FDR)<0.05 two-sided); 80-86% (association) and 46-77% (prefrontal) of whole-brain significant time-points also significant in individual regions.

questions.q: What are the privacy implications: can decoding succeed without subject cooperation?
questions.answer: Cross-subject decoders (anatomically aligned, n=7) perform barely above chance and significantly worse than within-subject (q(FDR)<0.05). Resistance tasks (naming animals, telling different story) significantly lower decoding in all cortical regions (q(FDR)<0.05 paired t-test). Cooperation required for both training and application.

questions.q: What training/evaluation conditions are only documented in the code repository, not the paper?
questions.answer: Random seed=42; 15 default training sessions (omitting 1,13,16,17,19); beam width=200, extensions=5, LM_MASS=0.9, LM_RATIO=0.1, NM_ALPHA=2/3, LM_TIME=8; 10 null sequences for window evaluation; GPT layer=9, context=5; separate imagined/perceived GPT checkpoints; word rate ROI selection by experiment; cuda devices; eval WINDOW=20.

questions.q: What caveats do the authors concede about decoder limitations?
questions.answer: High WER (0.92-0.94) — decoder paraphrases rather than recovers exact words; model misspecification (suboptimal semantic features) is major error source evidenced by concreteness correlation (ρ=0.14-0.27); future developments might bypass cooperation requirements; inaccurate predictions could be maliciously misinterpreted.
